summary: We study decentralized multi-agent target search where homogeneous agents communicate intermittently at Poisson-distributed times. Standard unconditional belief fusion wastes communication opportunities by synchronizing agents during high-entropy exploration, when diverse independent beliefs provide better coverage than a premature consensus. We introduce \emph{entropy-gated belief coordination}, in which agents skip fusion while their collective entropy ratio exceeds a threshold~\(θ\) and merge only during exploitation, consistent with the bifurcation structure of nonlinear opinion dynamics and the submodular structure of the per-step information gain objective. We further derive \(\Istep(α,β)\), the expected mutual information per observation step between two agents' binary sensors, as an interpretable, communication-free measure of sensor informativeness that motivates the gating design and guides system-level analysis. Experiments across 103{,}680 trials (nine grid sizes up to \(100{\times}100\), Poisson communication timing, four target movement patterns) show that the Entropy-Gated Trust-Decay Planner (\textsc{EG-TDP}), which adds a detection-probability planner switch in exploitation mode, achieves mean belief quality \(\bar{Q}=0.300\) (mean belief mass at the true target cell, averaged across all trials and steps), a \(58.9\%\) gain over arithmetic mean and a \(37.4\%\) gain over visit-weighted fusion. On representative configurations, EG-TDP also outperforms a joint-Bayesian reference that uses all agents'~observations at every step, despite operating under random intermittent contact only.

summary: Multi-agent coordination often requires strategic agents to share sensitive information about their states or objectives, creating a tension between performance and privacy. Our paper studies this tradeoff in stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) dynamic games with heterogeneous agent objectives. In our framework, agents share noise-perturbed state and reference information with a cloud computer that computes feedback Nash equilibrium strategies, with the injected noise calibrated to provide differential privacy. We derive an analytical expression for each agent's infinite-horizon steady-state cost of privacy relative to the non-private game. Then, we prove that when agents' objectives are sufficiently aligned, the injection of privacy noise necessarily incurs a positive performance cost. In contrast, we characterize a class of games with sufficiently misaligned objectives across agents for which an agent's cost of privacy can be strictly negative. Thus, counterintuitively, noise can simultaneously protect privacy and improve the equilibrium performance of an agent when the objectives of interacting agents are sufficiently misaligned. Finally, we present numerical experiments which corroborate our theoretical contributions.

summary: This record provides the public reproducibility materials associated with the study The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London’s Cultural Infrastructure . The repository contains analytical code, public-safe derived neighbourhood data, spatial weights, source provenance, methodological protocols, confirmatory and robustness outputs, joint spatial re-estimation results, and supplementary materials for 4,994 Greater London 2021 LSOAs and a 2022 common-vintage cultural-infrastructure dataset. The study measures proximity-weighted availability of recorded cultural infrastructure and distinguishes Production from Encounter/Presentation functions. The two functions strongly overlap spatially. Their most consistently detected direct difference concerns metropolitan centrality: both decline with distance from London’s Central Activities Zone, with a steeper Encounter gradient. The differential deprivation association is model- and construct-sensitive, while the density difference remains unresolved. Cultural sustainability is treated as a bounded implication of the observed infrastructure configuration rather than as a directly measured sustainability outcome. The repository excludes raw site-level address/UPRN data and copyrighted source documents. Exact source provenance, reconstruction instructions, checksums, component-specific rights information, and reproducibility metadata are included.
title: Data, Code and Reproducibility Materials for "The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London's Cultural Infrastructure"

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: The existential theory of the reals asks whether polynomial constraints with integer coefficients have a real solution. We give a proof placing this problem in the counting hierarchy. The first argument is intended to expose the essential steps: a coercive minimum reduces feasibility to a finite critical algebra; residue formulas give its multiplication traces; and a short collection of derivative signs selects a real root. Exact formal power series and univariate resultants complete the calculation. This proof permits singular critical fibers and does not require a multivariate resultant algorithm. A separate analysis lowers the bound to \(\ETR\subseteq\BPP^{\Clevel3}\subseteq\Clevel4\). It uses a common formal homotopy, ordered labels for real roots, and randomized integer-sign reconstruction. For each fixed \(w\), sentences with \(w\) alternating real quantifier blocks lie in \(\Clevel{9w+17}\). We then treat exact semidefinite feasibility, \(\PosSLP\), square-root sum, geometric real counting, Euler characteristic, and complex feasibility in separate applications. The corresponding bounds include \(\BPP^{\Clevel2}\) for general SDP, \(\BPP^{\PP}\cap\Pclass^{\NP^{\PP}}\) for \(\PosSLP\) and square-root sum, and \(\FP^{\Clevel4}\) for total geometric real counting. Longer arithmetic proofs, conditional certificate routes, and limitations of other approaches are collected in the supplementary sections.

summary: Replication package for “Supporting Carbon Pricing Markets with Probabilistic Cash Rebates.” This record contains the anonymized experimental data and Stata code required to reproduce the empirical results reported in the manuscript. The study consists of two incentivized online experimental waves examining purchasing behavior and carbon-emission offsets under carbon pricing and probabilistic cash rebates. Wave 1 was preregistered in the AEA RCT Registry under AEARCTR-0015002 . The supplemental Wave 2 study was preregistered separately under AEARCTR-0017601 . The replication package was validated using StataNow 19.5 MP on Windows 64-bit . Running MAINsyntax.do reproduces the principal analyses, robustness analyses, and generated figures. Detailed replication instructions are provided in README.md . The uploaded ZIP is the validated public replication package accompanying the manuscript.
title: Replication package for "Supporting Carbon Pricing Markets with Probabilistic Cash Rebates"

summary: This repository contains five human-labeled benchmark datasets developed for the study 'Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models' . The datasets support evaluation of automated methods for literature screening, structured information extraction in knowledge synthesis, and scientific data discovery. The repository includes: Literature screening — machine learning in concrete materials science: 440 publications, including 272 labeled relevant and 168 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_ml_in_concrete.csv Literature screening — nanopore transport using molecular dynamics simulations: 205 publications, including 40 labeled relevant and 165 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_nanopore_transport.csv Literature screening — lithium extraction using NASICON-type materials: 200 publications, including 15 labeled relevant and 185 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_lithium_extraction.csv Knowledge synthesis — machine learning in concrete materials science: human labels for 50 full-text publications across five structured information fields: machine learning task, algorithm, binder system, prediction target, and input feature. knowledge_synthesis_extraction_human_labels_ml_in_concrete.csv Data discovery — silicate glass density: 200 publications, including 89 labeled as containing the target data and 111 labeled as not containing the target data. Supporting evidence for glass composition and density is also provided. data_discovery_human_labels_silicate_glass_density.csv The literature screening benchmark datasets provide DOI, publication year, title, abstract, and human relevance label. A label of  TRUE indicates that a publication was judged relevant according to the corresponding inclusion and exclusion criteria, whereas FALSE indicates that it was judged not relevant. The data discovery dataset uses the same binary labeling convention to indicate whether a publication contains the specified silicate glass density data. For the knowledge synthesis dataset, human annotations were assigned to five structured information fields using predefined controlled vocabularies. Details of benchmark construction, inclusion and exclusion criteria, annotation procedures, and inter-annotator agreement are provided in the Supplementary Information of the associated study.   Citation If you use these datasets, please cite both the associated publication and this repository: Li, Z., He, Q., Chen, W., Yang, K., & Gong, K. (2026). Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models [Preprint]. alphaXiv. https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2609.automating-literature-screening-llms Li, Z., He, Q., Chen, W., Yang, K., & Gong, K. (2026).  Human-labeled benchmarks for automated literature screening and knowledge synthesis [Dataset]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21853689

summary: Replication package for "Pricing Permanence: Settlement Charges and Refugee Sorting." The paper studies the United Kingdom's proposed settlement charge of about £10,000 per adult asylum-support recipient, collected from earnings above a threshold. It uses a six-destination Roy model of refugee destination choice with logit tastes. The package contains the derived data, the full calibration and estimation pipeline (minimum-distance estimation of the taste scale on Sweden's 2013 permanence expansion and Danish benefit reforms), all counterfactual and robustness scripts, the stored result files, and a verifier that checks every number reported in the manuscript and its Online Supplement against those result files. Start with REPLICATION_README.md; bash run_all.sh verify reproduces the checks. Third-party source data are documented with their access dates and licenses in the data catalog; files that cannot be redistributed are listed with download instructions.
tags: refugee policy, self-selection, settlement, skill portability, income-contingent loans.

summary: This repository contains the computational code, numerical inputs, output tables, and audit records supporting the study “Electrothermal Modelling, Detectability, and Robustness of a Rhombohedral GeTe Thin-Film Dual-Mode Sensor: A Literature-Constrained Multiphysics Study". The package provides the reproducible workflow used for the revised electrothermal calculations, including electrical power-budget analysis, three-dimensional thermal reconstruction, transient-response calculations, thermal-boundary sensitivity, contact-resistivity sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and supporting verification records. The repository is intended to enable independent reproduction and inspection of the computational results reported in the manuscript. The study is literature-constrained and computational; the deposited files should not be interpreted as experimental calibration of a fabricated GeTe device
title: Reproducibility Package for "Electrothermal Modelling, Detectability, and Robustness of a Rhombohedral GeTe Thin-Film Dual-Mode Sensor: A Literature-Constrained Multiphysics Study"

summary: This article provides a comprehensive hygienic assessment of traditional and modern disinfection and purification methods used to supply the population with clean and safe drinking water. It analyzes the microbiological and epidemiological efficacy, impact on human health, and mechanisms affecting the organoleptic and toxicological properties of water associated with chemical (chlorination, ozonation), physical (ultraviolet radiation), and physicochemical (membrane filtration, reverse osmosis) technologies. Based on the current sanitary-hygienic standards of the Republic of Uzbekistan and World Health Organization recommendations, the article proposes the safest combined technological solutions for centralized and local water treatment facilities.
tags: drinking water, disinfection, chlorination, ozonation, ultraviolet radiation, reverse osmosis, hygienic assessment, trihalomethanes, epidemiological safety.
title: HYGIENIC ASSESSMENT OF INDOOR AIR QUALITY

summary: This research-software note introduces InstiAct v0.4.6, an independent Python framework for representing institutional admissibility and institutional state transitions in computational models. The note develops the modeling proposition that institutional structures can be represented as an explicit, inspectable, and experimentally variable state that filters candidate actions and can itself change through institutional events. It defines the boundary between institutional admissibility and physical feasibility, operational constraints, behavioral choice, learning, and optimization; documents the executable semantics of rights, hard constraints, defeasible norms, contracts, amendments, remedies, and transactions; and describes the interface for coupling InstiAct to agent-based models. DAMMAGE is treated as an explicit intellectual antecedent for executable rights-and-obligations environments, while InstiAct is positioned conservatively as an independent research implementation rather than a port, reconstruction, or claim of implementation equivalence. The note documents the v0.4.6 software release and supports reproducible computational experiments on institutional dynamics and changing action spaces.
title: InstiAct: An Executable Institutional Layer for Agent-Based and Computational Modeling — From Agreement Structures to Dynamic Action Spaces

It defines the boundary between institutional admissibility and physical feasibility, operational constraints, behavioral choice, learning, and optimization; documents the executable semantics of rights, hard constraints, defeasible norms, contracts, amendments, remedies, and transactions; and describes the interface for coupling InstiAct to agent-based models. DAMMAGE is treated as an explicit intellectual antecedent for executable rights-and-obligations environments, while InstiAct is positioned conservatively as an independent research implementation rather than a port, reconstruction, or claim of implementation equivalence. The note documents the v0.4.6 software release and supports reproducible computational experiments on institutional dynamics and changing action spaces.
title: InstiAct: An Executable Institutional Layer for Agent-Based and Computational Modeling — From Agreement Structures to Dynamic Action Spaces

summary: OpenAI’s October 2026 mathematics release raises a question about scholarly infrastructure: how can researchers make work public promptly while supporting scrutiny, durable citation and practical reuse? This article applies an earlier framework for research-archive release architecture to the GitHub release, arXiv’s moderation and submission limits, and Zenodo’s deposit and versioning arrangements. It distinguishes the authority to permit initial publication from the work of assessing a result. A repository’s limited evaluation capacity warrants attention, but does not by itself establish an appropriate limit on scientific production. Immediate release also creates responsibilities for producers, including clear verification status, usable exposition, stable references and support for subsequent understanding. A documented transfer difficulty and a reproducible inventory of 10,023 preprints files connect these institutional questions to practical access; repository-relative paths reach 271 characters, although the cause of the reported failure remains unresolved. The article proposes combining prompt public release with archived snapshots, explicit correction histories and independently organized scrutiny. GitHub and Zenodo can perform complementary roles, while persistent identifiers help readers locate the particular research object being discussed.
title: Making AI Research Public: Immediate Release, Scholarly Scrutiny and Durable Citation

summary: Deep generative models often produce structured outputs composed of interacting components. Modelling these outputs with a single model requires learning both the component distributions and their interactions. We pursue a modular alternative: reuse independently trained component generators and learn only how to coordinate them to produce coherent structured outputs. Our framework, Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering (CMDS), treats frozen pretrained diffusion models as reusable generative primitives and coordinates their reverse processes through a learned control. We formulate coordination as a stochastic optimal control problem, balancing an assembly-level reward that specifies the desired properties of the combined output against deviations from the pretrained dynamics. The learned control amortises this optimisation, allowing reuse across new task instances. Experiments show that CMDS can recover a known target distribution, satisfy different spatial constraints with the same trained control, and recover individual sources from degraded mixtures. Across multi-agent maze navigation, articulated robot planning, and text-conditioned human motion, CMDS turns frozen models into coordinated multi-agent generators.
title: One for All, All for One: Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering via Stochastic Optimal Control

summary: World models are usually judged from the inside: by prediction loss, by the return a policy earns in imagination, or by how convincing their frames look. We judge one from the outside. We learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, every hero acting every tick, games of up to 6,000 ticks), train a policy only inside it with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes, and measure that policy in the real game against the opponent the game ships with. The real game never provides a gradient; it provides the policy's own games as training data for the world model, and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy. Run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop, the policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421 of 600; 95% CI 66.4-73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, up from 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins none as dire, and neither does the shipped opponent when it plays itself. Four findings explain the result. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: every unanchored run collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric tracked the collapse. A world model that is accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy's own games, and Dyna repairs it there, which is worth +9.2 points of real win rate with the policy recipe held fixed. Finally, the policy inherits its world model's fidelity profile mechanic by mechanic: the model represents the macro game but not crowd control, cast timing or lethality, and the policy wins by map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting. We release the world model, the dream-PPO harness, a world-model debugger, the evaluation protocol, and every policy and log.
title: Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.
title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning

summary: Multi-agent coordination often requires strategic agents to share sensitive information about their states or objectives, creating a tension between performance and privacy. Our paper studies this tradeoff in stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) dynamic games with heterogeneous agent objectives. In our framework, agents share noise-perturbed state and reference information with a cloud computer that computes feedback Nash equilibrium strategies, with the injected noise calibrated to provide differential privacy. We derive an analytical expression for each agent's infinite-horizon steady-state cost of privacy relative to the non-private game. Then, we prove that when agents' objectives are sufficiently aligned, the injection of privacy noise necessarily incurs a positive performance cost. In contrast, we characterize a class of games with sufficiently misaligned objectives across agents for which an agent's cost of privacy can be strictly negative. Thus, counterintuitively, noise can simultaneously protect privacy and improve the equilibrium performance of an agent when the objectives of interacting agents are sufficiently misaligned. Finally, we present numerical experiments which corroborate our theoretical contributions.
title: The Cost of Differential Privacy in Linear-Quadratic Dynamic Games

summary: The existential theory of the reals asks whether polynomial constraints with integer coefficients have a real solution. We give a proof placing this problem in the counting hierarchy. The first argument is intended to expose the essential steps: a coercive minimum reduces feasibility to a finite critical algebra; residue formulas give its multiplication traces; and a short collection of derivative signs selects a real root. Exact formal power series and univariate resultants complete the calculation. This proof permits singular critical fibers and does not require a multivariate resultant algorithm. A separate analysis lowers the bound to \(\ETR\subseteq\BPP^{\Clevel3}\subseteq\Clevel4\). It uses a common formal homotopy, ordered labels for real roots, and randomized integer-sign reconstruction. For each fixed \(w\), sentences with \(w\) alternating real quantifier blocks lie in \(\Clevel{9w+17}\). We then treat exact semidefinite feasibility, \(\PosSLP\), square-root sum, geometric real counting, Euler characteristic, and complex feasibility in separate applications. The corresponding bounds include \(\BPP^{\Clevel2}\) for general SDP, \(\BPP^{\PP}\cap\Pclass^{\NP^{\PP}}\) for \(\PosSLP\) and square-root sum, and \(\FP^{\Clevel4}\) for total geometric real counting. Longer arithmetic proofs, conditional certificate routes, and limitations of other approaches are collected in the supplementary sections.
title: ETH in CH

summary: This repository contains the computational code, numerical inputs, output tables, and audit records supporting the study “Electrothermal Modelling, Detectability, and Robustness of a Rhombohedral GeTe Thin-Film Dual-Mode Sensor: A Literature-Constrained Multiphysics Study". The package provides the reproducible workflow used for the revised electrothermal calculations, including electrical power-budget analysis, three-dimensional thermal reconstruction, transient-response calculations, thermal-boundary sensitivity, contact-resistivity sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and supporting verification records. The repository is intended to enable independent reproduction and inspection of the computational results reported in the manuscript. The study is literature-constrained and computational; the deposited files should not be interpreted as experimental calibration of a fabricated GeTe device

summary: Scripts, data files and a browsable gene-map atlas for the article "Wetland-root microbial genomes contain recurrent multi-gene neighborhoods with potential relevance to naphthenic acid fractional compound transformation". Scripts cover MAG recovery and abundance, Prokka annotation, phylogenomics, a curated 667-protein reference-panel BLASTP screen of 365 genomes, candidate genomic-neighborhood reconstruction, iTOL dataset generation, architecture signatures, annotation confirmation, ROW versus OSPW comparison, and figure generation. Data files include the reference panel, BLASTP best-hit tables, candidate-neighborhood tables, the unified phylogenomic tree with iTOL annotation files, and Prokka annotations of all 365 genomes. The gene-map atlas (docs/) is viewable at https://julius-nweze.github.io/NAFC_genomic_neighborhoods/.
title: NAFC genomic-neighborhood analysis scripts, data and gene-map atlas

summary: This record provides the reproducibility archive accompanying the manuscript “Frontier Mutual Information: Structured Global Inference from Local Contrasts” by Tsutomu Mori and Takashi Kawamura. The manuscript develops frontier mutual information as a framework for structured local-to-global inference, investigating when informative local contrasts can be used to recover or constrain global mutual information. This archive contains the computational materials supporting the study, including source code, synthetic data, reference outputs, publication-figure generation materials, paper-to-artifact mappings, documentation, and integrity and verification files. It also includes materials for independent verification of the numerical and finite-sample results reported in the manuscript. The archive is intended to enable transparent inspection, independent reproduction, and verification of the computational results. The theoretical claims, assumptions, and scope of applicability should be interpreted according to the accompanying manuscript.
title: Frontier Mutual Information: Structured Global Inference from Local Contrasts — Reproducibility Archive

summary: This volume develops the epistemological and research-practical foundations required for Generative Relational Economics. It examines how relational realities become accessible through evidence, manifestation, representation, interpretation, judgment, and historically situated inquiry, while maintaining a distinction between what is observed or represented and the relational structures inferred from those manifestations. The epistemological analysis addresses evidential mediation, uncertainty, salience, interpretation, representation, model dependence, inverse inference, and historical re-epistemization. Knowledge is treated as a relational achievement whose validity depends upon the interaction among objects of inquiry, observers, methods, institutions, records, and interpretive contexts. The volume then develops research as praxis. Historical, interpretive, qualitative, quantitative, empirical, formal, and computational approaches are treated as partially irreducible modes of epistemic access rather than as components of a universal methodological hierarchy. Their relations may involve complementarity, tension, mutual correction, and revision. The final portion develops a methodology of relational inquiry concerned with entities, relations, processes, events, states, properties, boundaries, memberships, networks, and historically evolving relational structures. Particular attention is given to the identification of relational objects, comparison across contexts, temporal reconstruction, representation, evidence, and the limits of relational attribution. The result is an epistemological and methodological architecture for studying relational economic systems without reducing them either to isolated entities or to a single privileged mode of representation.

summary: This repository contains processed data, Python scripts, computational results, molecular structures, figures, and quality-control reports supporting the associated manuscript. The study integrates molecular identity verification, experimental solubility harmonization, temperature-model comparison, solvent safety, health and environmental evidence, and residue–bioactive associations. The molecular library includes 17 bioactive compounds and 10 solvents associated with five agro-food residue matrices. The current curated database contains 911 records. The three-model temperature benchmark uses an earlier, explicitly identified input version comprising 251 eligible measurements across 41 systems. Separate analyses document quercetin exclusion sensitivity, reference-temperature coverage, solvent-ranking sensitivity, and the exclusion of 12 chlorogenic-acid mixture records from principal composition-based comparisons. The README identifies input versions, analysis boundaries, and the software environment. Historical results are retained in versioned directories. Complete package execution has not been independently verified. Publisher articles and downloaded article XML files are not included. The calculations describe equilibrium solubility and conditional solvent-capacity scenarios; they do not establish matrix-specific extraction yields or validated functional products. Experimental source publications are identified through DOI and provenance fields.
title: Data and Code for "From Agro-Food Waste to Functional Ingredients: A Computational Framework for Green Solvent Selection and Bioactive Compound Recovery"

summary: Doucette’s paper asks what a single scalar time series can establish about the distinction between thin and thick chaos. Standard methods—delay reconstruction and estimated Lyapunov exponents—show local instability but not transport between coherent sets. The paper proves that transport statistics defined by set membership, such as residence times and switching counts, survive injective delay embedding. However, if the observable is symmetric under a system symmetry, symmetry-related sets become indistinguishable, and their reconstructed images coincide. A two-state reduction gives switching rates and the second eigenvalue of the transition matrix, with a test of whether the reduced Markov description is valid. A record containing no switches can certify thinness only weakly: under a Poisson assumption, it bounds the switching rate and supports claims only over horizons much shorter than the record itself. Data from the thin side of a crisis cannot determine where the crisis occurs, because the crisis depends on a basin boundary the attractor does not visit; a measurable gap can help only if its critical value is supplied from a model or calibration. The Chua circuit is the test case. Immediately on either side of the merging crisis, the Lyapunov exponent is similar, but switching between scrolls is absent below the crisis. The transfer-matrix protocol recovers the scrolls when residence times exceed roughly six loop periods, but fails for faster switching or for a symmetric observable. A thin-side gap forecast the crisis to within about 0.002 when the critical gap came from the model, and was uninformative otherwise. The paper also tests noise, drift, and stationarity. Limitations include simulated data, one thin-regime system, partition dependence, a Poisson assumption, and biased Lyapunov estimates. The conclusion is that a single series can show chaos and sometimes transport between coherent sets, but only with a suitable observable, slow exchange, and careful attention to what data cannot decide.

summary: Doucette’s paper asks what a single scalar time series can establish about the distinction between thin and thick chaos. Standard methods—delay reconstruction and estimated Lyapunov exponents—show local instability but not transport between coherent sets. The paper proves that transport statistics defined by set membership, such as residence times and switching counts, survive injective delay embedding. However, if the observable is symmetric under a system symmetry, symmetry-related sets become indistinguishable, and their reconstructed images coincide. A two-state reduction gives switching rates and the second eigenvalue of the transition matrix, with a test of whether the reduced Markov description is valid. A record containing no switches can certify thinness only weakly: under a Poisson assumption, it bounds the switching rate and supports claims only over horizons much shorter than the record itself. Data from the thin side of a crisis cannot determine where the crisis occurs, because the crisis depends on a basin boundary the attractor does not visit; a measurable gap can help only if its critical value is supplied from a model or calibration. The Chua circuit is the test case. Immediately on either side of the merging crisis, the Lyapunov exponent is similar, but switching between scrolls is absent below the crisis. The transfer-matrix protocol recovers the scrolls when residence times exceed roughly six loop periods, but fails for faster switching or for a symmetric observable. A thin-side gap forecast the crisis to within about 0.002 when the critical gap came from the model, and was uninformative otherwise. The paper also tests noise, drift, and stationarity. Limitations include simulated data, one thin-regime system, partition dependence, a Poisson assumption, and biased Lyapunov estimates. The conclusion is that a single series can show chaos and sometimes transport between coherent sets, but only with a suitable observable, slow exchange, and careful attention to what data cannot decide.

summary: What's new Interface (optional, pip install "eprdating[gui]" ) Interactive interface for Jupyter and Google Colab: equivalent dose, sediment gamma spectrometry and age in three tabs, with downloads of results and settings. Intensity window centred on a g value or on a field in G or mT; Compare methods gives De with the four intensity methods. Weights of the dose-response fit: measured errors, 1/I² or equal. Spectra Reader for Freiberg Instruments MS5000 spectra (ESRStudio .xml , .csv export, or a folder of runs). Double integral with the derivative baseline fitted outside the window: about 40 % less scatter. empirical_template : line-shape template from the strongest spectra of a series. Optional protocol for enamel fragments measured at several angles: merged spectrum, angular profile, X-ray calibration (the isotropic correction is not included). Dose rate Optional alpha escape at the enamel surfaces ( ToothSample(alpha_escape=True) ): brings unstripped ROSY reference ages to within 0.5–2.5 %. Validation Public dose series of the Calio P4 enamel (Hakim et al. 2025, Nature; CC-BY 4.0) included and tested: SSE De 2259–2286 Gy vs published 2267 ± 99 Gy, once the 8000 and 15 000 Gy labels of the archive are exchanged. Documentation Quick start from spectra to De with the functions; the interface is optional. Full list: CHANGELOG.md.

summary: Replication archive for the agent-based model reported in: Artıktay, G. G. (2026). Synthetic Abundance, Scarce Attention, and Platform Governance: An Agent-Based Model of AI-Generated Music in Streaming Markets (manuscript under review). The model studies how a platform-mediated streaming market converts AI-generated uploads into listening, payment, and revenue under alternative governance regimes (provenance detection with error, recommender demotion or exclusion, monetization and popularity recycling of bot streams, royalty thresholds, licensing splits, and listener-facing labels), with a particular interest in the gap disclosed by Deezer in 2026 between the upload share of fully AI-generated tracks (44%, then above 50%) and their stream share (1 to 3%). Version 1.2.1. No model code changed and every deposited output of version 1.2.0 is unchanged. This version completes the replication material of the revised design: the scripts behind the paired welfare comparisons (python/paired_welfare_v2.py), the twelve-month-window entry-shock trajectory (python/shock_window_v2.py) and the manuscript figures (python/figures_v2.py), their outputs, a codebook for outputs_v2/ (outputs_v2/README.md), the ODD protocol of the revised design (docs/ODD_protocol_v1.2.md), a fix to python/sensitivity_structure_v2.py (it now creates its output folder and accepts an output directory argument), and updated documentation. The whole pipeline was rerun from this archive on a second machine (Linux, Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, SALib 1.6) and every output file was identical to the deposited one. Contents: Python model (python/abm_music.py), scenario definitions (python/scenarios_v2.py), pipeline (python/run_pipeline_v2.py), Sobol and Latin-hypercube sensitivity analysis (python/sobol_v2.py), structural test (python/sensitivity_structure_v2.py), verification tests, the NetLogo replication of the version 1.1.0 design, every output file behind the manuscript's tables and figures (outputs_v2/), and documentation (README.md, CHANGELOG.md, docs/). Licence: CC BY 4.0.
title: ABM-AI-Music-Streaming: Replication archive for "Synthetic Abundance, Scarce Attention, and Platform Governance"

summary: FHR File Converter v0.3.0 converts and validates FAIR Header Reference genome metadata in JSON, YAML, FASTA, GFA and HTML microdata. This release packages the schema and eight CLI commands and supports optional assembly software provenance, protocol URI, N90/GC percentage and a supplied GA4GH SeqCol digest. Corrected conversion, combine, strip and checksum handling preserves metadata and non-FHR sequence bytes. Input overwrite checks include hard links. Microdata fixes cover independent scope isolation, standard machine-readable values, void elements and Unicode round trips. Migration: regenerate legacy MD5 or payload-only checksums. The v0.3 checksum is padded base64 SHA-512/256 over all exact file bytes except the scalar root checksum line and its terminator. Numeric schemaVersion remains 1. Use keyword constructor arguments; optional fields are absent until supplied. SeqCol identity is preserved, not computed. Sequence helpers read complete files into memory; checksum operations require Python SHA-512/256 support. GitHub release and wheel/source distributions ; companion specification archive ; published paper . Validation includes 39 regression tests and Python 3.9/3.13 CI. This archive and GitHub release do not imply publication to PyPI. The independent conduct/conflict reporting route remains a documented follow-up in specification issue #23.

summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . Keywords: Abstract algebra, cyclic groups, direct products, exponent coordinates, re- lation lattices, projection functors, natural transformations, Newton identities, Chinese Remainder Theorem, rank complexity. summary: This dataset supports the study “A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection.” It contains accession-level manifests, derived statistical tables, figure-source data, documentation, software-version information, and analysis code supporting an assembly-first workflow with raw-read reconstruction for publicly available sequencing records. Starting from 44,278 geographically resolved eligible records, 1,687 records had no analyzable public genome input, leaving 42,591 records with an analyzable genome input. Of these, two were excluded during final cohort harmonization, resulting in a final analytical collection of 42,589 K. pneumoniae genomes. This collection comprised 40,093 genomes represented by usable public assemblies and 2,496 genomes reconstructed from publicly available sequencing reads. The deposit does not redistribute genome assemblies or raw sequencing reads. Sequence data should be retrieved from the relevant public repositories using the accession identifiers provided in the manifests. The archived materials support reproduction of the post-assembly cohort audit, statistical summaries, and figures. The exact raw-read preprocessing commands used for the rescued genomes were not retained; consequently, adapter-trimming and quality-filtering parameters are not represented as reproducible components of this deposit. Reconstructed and deposited assemblies were nevertheless evaluated using the same post-assembly quality-control criteria before inclusion in the final analytical collection. Jianhua Li and Jing Guo contributed equally to this work. Jing Chen is the corresponding author. Correspondence: dongqingfei@126.com . Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Xiamen Municipality (No. 3502Z202373092).
title: Data and analysis materials for: A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection

summary: Nota metodologica dell'Autore: I percorsi logici e le reti vettoriali tracciati in questo studio non trovano riscontro nella letteratura scientifica coeva. Tale assenza non è da considerarsi un'evidenza di inconsistenza storica, bensì il risultato dei limiti intrinseci dei metodi accademici tradizionali, i quali non hanno finora sviluppato gli strumenti interdisciplinari e computazionali necessari a mappare e decodificare queste connessioni. L'Autore è pienamente consapevole che, se valutati secondo i rigidi e iper-specializzati standard dell'ortodossia archeologica e linguistica odierna, tali path possano apparire del tutto non convenzionali o estranei ai paradigmi accettati.   https://www.luigiusai.it/ontology/rotta-aristeica/index.html   Obbligatorio studiare questo documento assieme al seguente: Usai, L. (2026). Dal Monolite Nuragico alla Rete Tribale Cosmopolita: Un Modello Multidirezionale per la Diaspora e gli Hub Transmarini Sardi nel Mediterraneo Antico. summary: Occupational heat exposure is an important health risk in construction, particularly in hot-arid climates where ambient heat, physical workload, protective clothing and restricted recovery interact. This pilot study developed a transparent Construction Heat and Hydration Risk Index (CHHRI) using de-identified environmental monitoring and administrative rotation records from a construction setting in Saudi Arabia. Quantitative analysis comprised a convenience pilot subset of 87 hourly heat-index observations from seven complete monitoring sheets. Heat index ranged from 31 to 55 (mean 46.6 ± 6.1); 74.7% of observations were in the operational Danger category and 17.2% in Extreme Danger. CHHRI integrates environmental heat severity, workload, PPE thermal burden, hydration deficit and recovery deficit on a 0–100 scale. Only the environmental component used observed quantitative data; the other four components were examined using 5,000 explicitly simulated, non-empirical scenarios. Baseline weights are provisional conceptual values, and alternative-weight sensitivity was evaluated. CHHRI is presented as a decision-support research prototype, not a validated predictor of heat illness.
title: Integrated Heat and Hydration Risk Framework for Construction Workers in Hot-Arid Environments

summary: This repository contains the machine-learning surrogate pipeline for predicting size-resolved aerosol particle number concentrations (nucleation, Aitken, and accumulation modes) from conventional atmospheric variables over Beijing. The pipeline implements a two-stage stacked ensemble: a CatBoost classifier that stratifies samples into low/high-concentration regimes, three base regressors (XGBoost, Random Forest, RBF-SVR) per regime, and a LightGBM meta-learner that stacks base-learner predictions with 26 raw predictors. Pre-trained weights for all three particle modes are included, along with the held-out test set and scripts to reproduce the reported R2 and Pearson correlation metrics. The target variable is transformed with Yeo-Johnson standardization; predictions are written in the transformed space, and the provided power transformer allows inverse transformation to physical units (cm-3).
title: Learning size-resolved aerosol number concentrations from conventional atmospheric variables: insights from Beijing

summary: Data accompanying N. Vauquier, B. M. L. Srivastava, S. A. Hosseini and E. Vincent, "Legally validated evaluation framework for voice anonymization", Interspeech 2025, pages 3229 to 3233, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2025-1699. The paper introduces two metrics, Singling Out and Linkability, that translate the singling out and linkability criteria of the Article 29 Working Party's Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymization Techniques into quantities that can be measured on speech. The framework was formally validated by the French Data Protection Authority (CNIL). This record holds the data needed to reproduce the paper's results. The reference implementation is at https://github.com/brijmohan/voice-anonymization-legal-eval CONTENTS Dataset definitions, unchanged from version 1.0.0: cv11-A-filelist (19.5 MB): the Mozilla Common Voice 11.0 clips forming subset A, 22,024 speakers with at least 2 minutes of speech each. cv11-B-filelist (83.3 MB): the clips forming subset B, 4,949 speakers with at least 3 minutes each. Subset B's speakers are a subset of A's, with disjoint utterances. Cosine score matrices, new in version 2.0.0, 12 files totalling 5.2 GB: scores_<attacker>_L<length>.npy: a 22,024 x 4,949 float32 array per attacker model and conversation length. Entry [i, j] is the cosine similarity between enrollment speaker i of subset A and test speaker j of subset B. scores_<attacker>_L<length>.npy.json: a sidecar per matrix giving the row and column speaker order, so each matrix is self describing. MANIFEST.json: SHA-256 checksums and shapes for every file. The four attacker models differ in what their speaker embedding extractor was trained on: original : original speech, evaluated on original speech. ignorant : original speech. semi_informed : speech anonymized with VoicePrivacy 2022 baseline B1.a. informed : speech anonymized with VoicePrivacy 2024 baseline B1. Conversation length L is the number of utterances averaged per speaker, and takes the values 1, 3 and 30. Test data for the three attackers is anonymized with VoicePrivacy 2024 baseline B1. USING THE MATRICES pip install git+https://github.com/brijmohan/voice-anonymization-legal-eval from legal_eval.io import load_score_matrix from legal_eval.sweeps import linkability_sweep m = load_score_matrix("scores_informed_L1.npy") print(linkability_sweep(m, speaker_counts=[20, 100, 1000, 10000]).mean()) To check a download against the published results: python examples/03_verify_against_score_matrices.py --release-dir . That recomputes all 2,640 published Linkability points. Expect a worst case difference of about 0.005, which is Monte Carlo noise from averaging five runs. WHAT THE MATRICES CONTAIN These are similarity scores rather than speaker embeddings, but the distinction is smaller than it sounds and it is worth being explicit. Each matrix is the product of two sets of unit norm x-vectors, so its rank is bounded by the embedding dimension rather than by its shape. Measured on a random 3,000 x 3,000 block, the singular value spectrum collapses by four orders of magnitude immediately after index 256, which is the x-vector dimension, and a rank 256 reconstruction reproduces the released scores to within 2e-07. A recipient can therefore recover similarity structure that was never released, link a speaker across the four released conditions, and cluster speakers by voice similarity. ON THE SPEAKER LABELS Row and column labels are internal pseudonyms of the form spk-f-20851, not Mozilla Common Voice client identifiers. They should not be relied on as a safeguard. The subset file lists in this record are public, Common Voice publishes a client identifier for every clip, and the evaluation pipeline is openly reproducible, so a determined party could recompute an original condition matrix and align it to the released one to recover the mapping. summary: This poster presents a lunar surface simulation framework and synthetic dataset for evaluating visual-domain zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in lunar perception. The framework integrates terrain reconstruction, lunar surface appearance modelling, realistic illumination, and synthetic data generation to support controlled evaluation of visual fidelity and cross-dataset segmentation performance. Experimental results show that the proposed dataset achieves lower feature-space distance to real lunar imagery and stronger zero-shot segmentation performance across multiple model architectures. The work further investigates mixed-training strategies and key simulation design factors. Presented at the Towards Sustainability and Resiliency of Field Robotics Workshop, IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2025), Hangzhou, China, 20 October 2025. Honourable Mention for Best Poster Award.
title: A Novel Lunar Surface Simulation Framework Enabling Visual Domain Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer

summary: Iris biometric authentication systems employ the exclusive texture patterns of the iris to identify an individual; they can be very stable over time and are well suited for secure identity verification applications. Protecting stored iris templates is difficult, however, because of privacy concerns, irreversible exposure to iris biometrics and diminished authentication confidence if the templates are compromised. For iris recognition, researchers have developed new techniques based on deep learning to achieve better performance in feature extraction and classification. Frequently, however, these methods have weak template security, lack of feature optimization, and lack of scalability for authentication in cloud-based environments. Thus, researchers proposed the ACH-CIR: Attention-Guided Hybrid CNN–ANN Framework for Secure Cancelable Iris Recognition in Cloud Computing Environments. The pre-processing of iris images is done by segmentation, normalization and enhancement techniques in ACH-CIR model which is based on USIT framework. It then transforms the data using secure cancelable transformation through BLAKE3 hashing, generation of user-specific seed-matrix, and inverse feature transformation for privacy preservation. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are used to extract features and an attention mechanism is further used to optimize the features. The hybrid deep learning integration consists of extracting the features using CNN and authentication using ANNs for iris authentication. Such metrics as accuracy, precision, recall, GAR, FAR, FRR and EER are used to measure performance. The proposed Attention-guided CNN–ANN model is able to provide better recognition accuracy and protection for template in standard CASIA iris datasets. The method could lead to a substantial enhancement of secure biometric authentication, as it allows for accurate, revocable and scalable iris recognition in cloud computing environments.

title: ACH-CIR: ATTENTION-GUIDED HYBRID CNN–ANN FRAMEWORK FOR SECURE CANCELABLE IRIS RECOGNITION IN CLOUD COMPUTING ENVIRONMENTS

summary: OWL v1.3.0 This release corrects the free-surface treatment in all 2D and 3D wave solvers and fixes several issues in 3D runs with MPI domain decomposition. Parameter files and output formats are unchanged. Free surface (acoustic, elastic iso/VTI/HTI/ORT, and elastic TTI solvers, 2D and 3D) Wavefield above the surface. The solvers now mirror the particle velocities above the free surface, v(−z) = v(z). Before, the top rows of the finite-difference stencils read zeros there. This made elastic surface amplitudes 6–8% too low at any mesh refinement and caused waveform errors of about 2% in acoustic media. Sources near the surface. A source whose interpolation stencil reaches the surface is injected together with its mirror image. A force is its own image. For an explosion or a moment tensor, the image removes the part that a traction-free surface cannot support. On the refined near-surface mesh, each stencil row is scaled by its own cell height. Before, the solvers dropped the stencil points on and above the surface, and force sources were not normalized by the cell height. In the elastic solvers, a source given above the surface is placed on it; this replaces the former relocation with an empirical amplitude factor. Receivers near the surface. Acoustic receivers whose interpolation stencil reaches above the surface now read the pressure mirrored about it, p(−z) = −p(z). Before, 3D receivers within four grid cells of the surface read zeros there (errors of a few percent), and 2D receivers read a mirror that missed the most recent source injection. FWI near the surface. The adjoint sources follow the same rule as the sources, which makes them the exact adjoint of the receiver sampling. In our tests, source–receiver reciprocity errors near the surface drop from up to 47% to about 10⁻⁵. In 2D acoustic media, the adjoint source no longer accumulates on the surface row, where the pressure must stay zero. The moment-tensor gradient is now the exact transpose of the moment-tensor source, including its mirror image and, in TTI media with topography, the cell scaling of each source column. Accuracy. Against an analytical half-space solution, for explosion, force, and moment-tensor sources at 1.25 m and 20 m depth, amplitudes agree within about 5% at receivers on the surface and within about 2% at 150 m depth (0.2% for the 20 m source). A source exactly on the surface is the worst case: up to about 5% (standard staggered grid) and 10% (fully staggered grid) at the surface receivers with the default 4× refinement. This first-order error halves with each doubling of the refinement. Acoustic results match the exact image solution to about 10⁻⁶. 3D runs with domain decomposition or several shot groups rankx and rankz now decompose the x- and z-axes. Before, they were swapped. FWI without energy preconditioning: the gradient was summed over the blocks of a shot only inside the energy preconditioning, so a decomposed run without it wrote only the block of rank 0. Elastic FWI with a free surface: the gradients of vp, vs, and the anisotropy parameters were zero outside the block of rank 0, because the chain rule took the density from that block only. The solvers now use the input density. FWI: the step length, the merged gradient, and the trace weights now count each shot group once. Before, they counted it once per rank of the group. FWI: the boundary records of the source-wavefield reconstruction are clipped consistently to each block, the restored final-step wavefield gets fresh halos, and halos are refreshed before snapshots and before the gradient computation. The density at force sources (all 3D solvers) and the stability check (TTI) are now reduced over the shot group instead of all ranks. With ngroup > 1, force amplitudes were divided by ngroup and the stable time step was overestimated. summary: The full transformation semigroup T n is a fundamental object in finite semigroup theory, and imposing restrictions on the fibres of its transformations gives rise to important structural subclasses. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of the perfect-preserving full transformation semigroup ,   a subclass of the full transformation semigroup T n consisting of all transformations f : X n   X n   where X n = {1,2,…,n}, satisfying the condition:   for every y in the image of   . The study aims to characterize the fundamental algebraic properties of   including its rank structure, idempotents, regularity, ideals, and Green's relations. An algebraic approach based on kernel block/partitions, image sets, rank, and function composition is employed to study the elements of . The regularity of the semigroup is established by constructing a perfect-preserving pseudo-inverse for an arbitrary element, while kernel and image classifications are used to investigate its Green classes and rank-based ideal structure. The results show that every element of is singular and has rank at most , while non-constant perfect-preserving transformations exist if and only if . The idempotents in are characterized as those idempotent transformations for which every fixed point has at least one additional preimage. Furthermore, its ideals are organised according to admissible ranks, with the constant transformations forming the minimal ideal, and its Green-class decomposition is described in terms of kernel and image structures. These results provide a foundation for further combinatorial and algebraic investigations of perfect-preserving transformation semigroups.
title: ALGEBRAIC STRUCTURE OF PERFECT-PRESERVING FULL TRANSFORMATION SEMIGROUP

summary: This dataset contains the experimental materials and retained research records supporting the master’s thesis on evaluating LLM-based identification of non-functional requirements (NFRs) from agile user stories. The dataset consists of two Excel files: Research_Experiment_Data_Final.xlsx This file contains the retained experimental records used in the study, including: reconstructed user stories and their provenance; human analyst NFR annotations; consensus voting and the resulting baseline NFRs; AI-generated NFR identification results from repeated GPT-4o-mini runs; AI consistency results across repeated runs; AI-human matching and adjudication results; timing observations for human and AI-based NFR identification; System Usability Scale (SUS) responses; per-evaluator and aggregate performance metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score. 25_reconstructed_stories_.xlsx This file contains the 25 reconstructed user stories used as the experimental input dataset. It documents the source material used for reconstruction, source URLs, source evidence, the rationale for reconstruction, and the resulting reconstructed user stories. The reconstructed stories were created for the experiment and should not be interpreted as verbatim quotations of the original source datasets. Together, these files provide the underlying experimental records and input materials necessary to understand and reproduce the quantitative analyses reported in the thesis. The dataset supports examination of human versus LLM-based NFR identification, including identification accuracy, consistency, agreement with the human-derived baseline, processing time, and usability. The data are provided for research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic analysis. Source publications referenced within the dataset remain the property of their respective copyright holders. The reconstructed user stories are experimental research materials derived from source-supported characteristics and are explicitly documented as reconstructed rather than presented as original source text.

summary: We develop a rigorous asymptotic-statistical theory for the inference of stochastic-belief extended realities (SBxRs), the path-space probabilistic objects introduced in [1] for the modelling of perceptual experience in extended-reality systems. Given n independent percept trajectories drawn from an SBxR with an unknown parameter θ0 ∈ Θ ⊂ Rd and a known modality-weight structure, we construct an importance-weighted plug-in estimator ˆgn of the aggregated Fisher–Rao metric g, prove its strong consistency and asymptotic normality under standard mixing-and-moment conditions on the per-modality Itˆo diffusions, and establish operator-norm concentration via matrix Bernstein. The aggregated maximum-likelihood estimator ˆθn is shown to be consistent and asymptotically efficient with limiting covariance g(θ0)−1, and the plug-in estimator ˆgn(ˆθn) inherits a delta-method-style central limit theorem. We then address the joint identifiability of the aggregation exponent p ∈ (1,∞] from the Lp-Fisher–Rao Finsler family of [4], proving that p is qualitatively identifiable under a non-collinearity condition on the per-modality Fisher matrices but that the Fisher information for p saturates as p → ∞, with a closed-form per-direction saturation point p⋆(ξ) = 1/ log(r1(ξ)/r2(ξ)) in terms of the typical ratio of largest to second-largest weighted per-modality Fisher contributions. The estimator ˆpK achieves the parametric rate K−1/2 uniformly on a bounded interval [1, peff ] determined by this saturation point but degrades to non-parametric rates beyond it. We provide a Le Cam two-point minimax lower bound matching the upper bound up to constants, extend the framework to non-Gaussian percept processes (jump-diffusions via Jacod–Shiryaev; fractional-Brownian percepts via Shimizu– Nakajima 2024), and prove the validity of an i.i.d. path-bootstrap. A JAX implementation and eight numerical experiments validate the theory on the trichromatic-color worked example of [1] and on synthetic non-Gaussian percept models. Keywords: Fisher information; Fisher–Rao metric; SBxR; path-
