summary: Review article. Introduction: Needs assessment according to Maslow’s theory is essential in clinical practice as it supports individualized care planning and patient-centered decision-making. Furthermore, it promotes a balanced therapeutic relationship between healthcare professionals and patients. The aim of this study was to explore Maslow’s theory in clinical settings and in nursing care. Methodology: A literature search of scientific articles was conducted in the electronic databases PubMed and Scopus. The keywords used included: “needs”, “patients”, and “Maslow’s hierarchy of needs”, along with their synonyms and combinations. Results: Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is applied across intensive care, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, rehabilitation, reconstructive surgery, cardiology and hemodialysis. The model is used to support holistic, patient-centered care by prioritizing physiological and safety needs while also addressing psychological, social, and self-actualization domains. Its application has been associated with improved recovery, symptom management, functional outcomes, self-management, treatment adherence, and quality of life. Findings indicate that higher-order needs remain relevant but are often secondary to physiological stabilization mainly in acute clinical contexts. Conclusions: The application of Maslow’s hierarchy provides a structured biopsychosocial framework for understanding patients’ needs and guiding individualized nursing interventions across diverse clinical settings, thereby supporting the delivery of comprehensive and person-centered care.
title: MASLOW'S HIERARCHY OF NEEDS IN CLINICAL SETTINGS AND IN NURSING CARE

summary: v1.0.0 — Initial Audited Analysis Code Release Initial public release of the audited analysis code supporting: Cross-Cohort Transportability, Calibration, and Incremental Value of Breast DCE-MRI Radiomics for Predicting Pathologic Complete Response Included Preprocessing and cohort preparation scripts DCE-MRI radiomics extraction workflow Clinical, radiomics, and combined modeling pipelines Internal and external validation scripts Bootstrap comparison analyses Figure-generation scripts Reproducibility and analysis-workflow documentation Version-pinned Python environment Reproducibility scope This release contains the audited analysis code and documentation used for the reported analyses. No patient-level data, medical images, masks, prediction files, or derived radiomics matrices are distributed in this repository. Three historical provenance gaps are explicitly documented in the repository and should be considered when interpreting end-to-end reproducibility. Data The analyses use publicly available breast DCE-MRI resources. Dataset access information and applicable licensing are documented in docs/DATA_AVAILABILITY.md . License Code in this repository is released under the MIT License. Dataset licenses remain governed by their respective data providers. Release: v1.0.0 Release date: 2026-10-08
title: Cross-Cohort Transportability, Calibration, and Incremental Value of Breast DCE-MRI Radiomics for Predicting Pathologic Complete Response

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FHR File Converter

summary: tdfpy is a Python package for reading Bruker timsTOF data from analysis.tdf and analysis.tdf_bin files inside a .d directory. It accesses the SQLite metadata and compressed binary peak data directly, so workflows do not need the Bruker native library. High-level readers represent data-dependent acquisition, data-independent acquisition, and parallel reaction monitoring runs through frames, precursors, isolation windows, targets, and transitions. Metadata is loaded when a run is opened, while raw peak arrays are decoded only when requested. Spectrum extraction can retain ion mobility as arrays of mass-to-charge ratio, intensity, and inverse reduced mobility. Processing pipelines support region exclusion, smoothing, configurable noise filters, and two centroiding approaches: greedy peak merging in floating-point mass space and watershed region growth in time-of-flight index space. Frames and acquisition objects can also be selected by identifiers, mass-to-charge ranges, and retention time. tdfpy is intended for proteomics workflows that need scriptable access to timsTOF measurements, mobility-resolved peaks, and PASEF acquisition metadata on Linux, macOS, or Windows.
title: tdfpy: A Python package for parsing and centroiding Bruker timsTOF mass spectrometry data

summary: This work investigated the capability of multilayer perceptron artificial neural network (MLP–ANN), stochastic gradient boosting (SGB) tree, radial basis function artificial neural network (RBF–ANN), and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) models to determine the heat capacity ( C p ) of ionanofluids in terms of the nanoparticle concentration ( x ) and the critical temperature ( T c ), operational temperature ( T ), acentric factor ( ω ), and molecular weight ( M w ) of pure ionic liquids (ILs). To this end, a comprehensive database of literature reviews was searched. The results of the SGB model were more satisfactory than the other models. Furthermore, an analysis was done to determine the outlying bad data points. It showed that most of the experimental data points were located in a reliable zone for the development of the model. The mean squared error and R 2 were 0.00249 and 0.987, 0.0132 and 0.9434, 0.0320 and 0.8754, and 0.0201 and 0.9204 for the SGB, MLP–ANN, ANFIS, and RBF–ANN, respectively. According to this study, the ability of SGB for estimating the C p of ionanofluids was shown to be greater than other models. By eliminating the need for conducting costly and time-consuming experiments, the SGB strategy showed its superiority compared with experimental measurements. Furthermore, the SGB displayed great generalizability because of the stochastic element. Therefore, it can be highly applicable to unseen conditions. Furthermore, it can help chemical engineers and chemists by providing a model with low parameters that yields satisfactory results for estimating the C p of ionanofluids. Additionally, the sensitivity analysis showed that C p is directly related to T , M w , and T c , and has an inverse relation with ω and x . M w and T c had the highest impact and ω had the lowest impact on C p .
title: Estimating the heat capacity of non-newtonian ionanofluid systems using ANN, ANFIS, and SGB tree algorithms

summary: Lean Verification for “Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling” — Version 2.0 Version 2.0 integrates the full Lean formalizations of A1–A4 into the uniform-hiding development accompanying Hongru Zhao’s manuscript. The four scientific axioms used by version 1.3.0 are removed and replaced by proved theorem/data declarations preserving their original full contracts. The public hiding theorem, quantitative corollary, dimension ranges and constants are unchanged. The integrated proofs establish: A1 — COE principal-block law: the exact Haar principal corner law, including the boundary dimension, with its literal determinant density and self-normalization. A2 — Takagi–Weyl integration: global spectrum measurability and the flat complex-symmetric integration law, with one positive finite constant for arbitrary measurable permutation-invariant tests and measurable target spaces. The historical A2Prime name is retained for compatibility. A3 — Gaussian GSVD beta-Jacobi law: the squared generalized-singular-value law on the original real and complex Gaussian pair carriers, including global coordinate measurability and the full original dimension range. A4 — Wishart tensor moments: both direct and inverse tensor-moment formulas with the original matching-Gram coefficient convention. The supplied Wishart probability law and its transform characterization remain explicit theorem hypotheses. The all-input uniform-hiding theorem covers every 1 ≤ N,K ≤ M , including K < N , at the bound min{1, 615172 N²/M} . Its normalized and unscaled product forms, Corollary 2.2 and source-scale (S62) specialization are retained. The assembled Route 1 relative-accuracy bounds use these integrated proofs and the included companion Gaussian anticoncentration development. Lean’s standard foundations— propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound —remain. The executable endpoint audits require exactly that foundation set. Removing the four scientific axioms does not remove the explicit probability-model, dimension or estimator hypotheses from the theorem statements. Fresh verification passed on 8 October 2026 (America/Chicago). The named public build and two separate Lean audit executions each returned exit code zero. The exact 18 provider/public endpoints passed, and the transitive inventory audited 19,639 imported local theorem declarations across 1,162 modules , from 1,241 current Lean source files , with zero scientific axioms . The allowed logical foundations are the three listed above. The fresh build invocation reused pinned dependencies and unaffected compiled-module caches; it was not a wholly uncached check or an independent checker run. The source-linked result and command logs are recorded in verification/FINAL_VERIFICATION.json . Historical September receipts retain their original snapshot meaning. Archive hashes and fresh-extraction checks establish package integrity separately from proof validation. The photon-sector normalization, generating function, passive photon-number conservation, optimized reference scale, average-TV sampler bound, Route 1 asymptotics and all-input applications from version 1.3.0 are preserved. The squeezed-vacuum coefficients, passive tensor action and collision-free hafnian probability are adopted optical-model definitions; deriving the full model from quantum dynamics remains outside this development. Route 2 remains a conditional deduction with an explicit symmetric-Gaussian matrix-comparison premise. This release does not claim a proof of the Shou comparison or complete actual-law Route 2 assembly. The companion symmetric-Gaussian small-ball theorem is available separately. The package contains Lean sources, pinned configuration, the portable verifier, documentation, source-to-manuscript correspondence, provenance and verification records. It preserves the original version 1.3.0 archive byte-f
title: Lean Verification for "Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling"

summary: Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC) both distribute Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance, and their outputs can be combined in a single time series. Over one 73 ha cattle farm in northern Colombia, we tested whether the two platforms yield the same parcel-scale vegetation and water indices and, where they differ, at which layer the difference originates: the product, the processing chain or the scene universe. For identical products, scene classification and harmonised reflectance matched in every comparable pixel, and the same chain executed locally or server-side in GEE gave per-scene indices and monthly medians that agreed within 1e-6. The catalogues, however, did not hold the same scenes: between June 2024 and April 2025, 10 of 146 scene–tile records existed only in GEE, six of them Sentinel-2C records, and none only in MPC; in 22 of 136 common records, all from June–July 2024, the catalogues held different L2A generations of the same acquisition. In the two monthly composites tested over the farm, the GEE-only scenes shifted mean NDVI by −0.0005 and −0.0087; over a public 1 km² demonstration area with the same scene inventory, the shift reached −0.028 (January 2025). Files: - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_preprint_v1.pdf — preprint (English), not peer reviewed. - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_data_v1.zip — reconciliation table with scene identifiers, processing baselines and cloud cover; E2 analysis; scene lists and SHA-256 hashes of each composite; monthly metrics and per-pixel difference distributions; evidence tables for Section 3.2; public demonstration area of interest and tool outputs on it. The farm geometry is not included (landowner privacy). - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_code_v1.0.0.zip — three Python tools (MIT licence), Spanish-language guide, acceptance test and workflow figures. Code in the software archive is released under the MIT licence. Catalogues queried on 24 September 2026. Developed within the Curso de Percepción Remota Avanzada, Doctorado en Agroecología, Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Sede Bogotá. Generative AI assistants (Claude, Anthropic; ChatGPT, OpenAI) supported test design, code, literature search, review and drafting; the author verified all results and is responsible for the content.
title: Same computation, different scenes: a single-site comparison of Sentinel-2 L2A composites from Google Earth Engine and Microsoft Planetary Computer

summary: This repository contains the curated research inputs, analysis code, and reference outputs supporting the study “Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings.” The study examines whether estimates of global irrigation savings depend on which suppliers reduce production, even when displacement quantities are held fixed within each market. It combines crop production, trade, and water-use data with constrained allocation models, historical production-contraction benchmarks, alternative water accounts, and conditional future scenarios for 2050 and 2100. Repository contents 01_Research_Inputs.xlsx — Curated source observations, geographic and crop identifiers, variable definitions, and source citations. 02_Research_Data.sqlite — Larger input datasets, archived analytical outputs, numerical checks, optional derived checkpoints, and an index linking the release to the associated manuscript and supplementary material. Source inputs and computed outputs are explicitly distinguished. 03_Analysis.py — Consolidated Python code containing the analytical modules, dependency specifications, input verification, and reproduction workflow. 04_Readme.txt — Documentation of data provenance, units, assumptions, reproduction instructions, licensing, and file checksums. The release corresponds to six main-text figures, 16 supplementary figures, and 24 supplementary tables. The exact associated manuscript and supplementary document versions are identified by their SHA-256 fingerprints. Data sources include ACEA, FAOSTAT, CWASI, GCAM scenario outputs, USGS irrigation water-use estimates, Kansas irrigation-technology replication data, and complementary water-account datasets. Source-specific citations and attribution requirements are retained in the documentation. Reproduction and validation The documented workflow uses Python 3.11. Separate dependency environments are specified where required. Installing dependencies requires internet access; the numerical analyses use the deposited inputs. Instructions cover the complete workflow and targeted reproduction checks. For version 1.0.1, file checksums, database integrity, and embedded assets were verified. The full-routing analysis was rerun from the deposited GCAM inputs for all 50 future configurations, reproducing the archived global water bounds and joint conservation outcomes within numerical tolerance. This targeted validation does not constitute a new execution of every stage of the study. Interpretation and reuse The modeled water bounds are conditional on specified technology responses, market quantities, supplier availability, production constraints, and water-use coefficients. They are not confidence intervals or globally identified causal effects of irrigation-technology adoption. Future configurations are conditional stress tests, not probabilistic forecasts. Original data compilations and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0, and original analysis code under the MIT License. Third-party inputs retain their source-specific licenses and attribution requirements, as documented in the README. Please cite this repository and the relevant original data sources when reusing the materials.
title: Data and code for "Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings"

summary: Code, 2.5-D finite-wavelength forward solver, datasets, trained models and result files reproducing every number in the manuscript "Source-Conditioned Neural Surrogates for Magnetotelluric Response Prediction Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation" (S. Oh). The study makes the magnetotelluric source an explicit input of a neural forward surrogate. A validated 2.5-D scattered-field solver for a source of finite along-strike wavelength generates the training data; a conditional U-Net predicts the electromagnetic fields, from which impedance and tipper are reconstructed; an aliasing ratio quantifies how much of a source perturbation a plane-wave inversion re-images as conductivity; a surrogate-domain recoverability experiment returns a source estimate close to the known synthetic value, while a direct solver re-forward shows that the recovered conductivity and wavenumber are not together a solver-consistent inverse solution; and magnetometer arrays at three geomagnetic latitudes place real settings on the dimensionless axis that the model defines. CONTENTS: README.md, LICENSE, DATA_LICENSE.txt and requirements.txt are attached unpacked. The code archive holds the analysis scripts (top level and mt3d/) and the full solver source (solver/, with the dataset generator, the Jacobian dump, the re-forward program and the unit tests); it is MIT licensed except the third-party Triangle library, which is redistributed verbatim under its own terms. The data archive holds the three datasets (dataset_dense, dataset_freq, dataset40), the trained checkpoints (ckpt/, mt3d/ckpt/), the joint-inversion and layered-earth training data (mt3d/*.npz), the plane-wave Jacobian dump (phase3/), the solver sweeps (phase1_repro/) and the result files next to the scripts that write them, all under CC BY 4.0 (DATA_LICENSE.txt). Figures and figure-drawing scripts are not included; every figure is a direct plot of a listed result file. Comments have been removed from all code written for this study. Not included: the magnetometer-array time series, which are third-party open data (EarthScope/USArray MT through the IRIS/EarthScope Data Management Center; AusLAMP Musgraves/APY through AuScope and Geoscience Australia, CC BY 4.0) and are rebuilt from those sources by the archived fetch and conversion scripts; and the field-station file that supplies the period list of the two control tests of Section S-XVII (available from the author on request).
title: Source-Conditioned Residual Learning for Magnetotelluric Responses Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation

summary: The critical exponent ν of Newton’s coupling is the main quantity compared between the functional renormalization group and lattice gravity. In a gauge-independent Einstein–Hilbert approximation it is known in closed form, and optimized regulators were reported to give ν ≈ 1/3, the value found in Regge-calculus simulations. Writing threshold functions as moments over the ratio u = p2/(p2 + Rk) of the regularized to the free propagator, we show that in this approximation 1/ν = (d − 2)(1 + ⟨u⟩), with ⟨u⟩ a weighted mean of u. In four dimensions, exchanging momentum and regulator maps 1/ν to 6 − 1/ν, so every shape function that is its own inverse, including Litim’s and the power-law regulator, gives ν = 1/3 exactly. Litim’s gap criterion is invariant under the exchange and leaves ν free: optimized regulators with finite threshold functions realize all 1/4 < ν < 1/2. The same mechanism acts in the minimal essential scheme: the condition on the inessential vacuum energy involves a threshold function dominated by the ultraviolet tail of the regulator. At second order in derivatives, standard optimized regulators give 1/ν between 2.31 and 2.49, and optimized regulators with longer ultraviolet tails reach the lattice value 1/ν ≈ 3.0. Choosing graviton and ghost regulators so that the vacuum term vanishes removes this dependence and leaves 1/ν between 2.19 and 2.73 for all shapes considered, below the lattice value.
title: The gravitational critical exponent and the shape of the regulator

summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

summary: Autoregressive video diffusion enables causal video streaming without a bidirectional pass over the full clip, but existing few-step systems usually retain only the opening and most recent frames in a fixed-size KV cache. Once an event leaves this window, later frames can no longer attend to it, a failure we term mid-horizon forgetting. We present Memory Forcing, a few-step streaming method that preserves this missing history without increasing the cache size. Its Archive \& Working Banks partition the cache into sink, archive, and working regions, retaining diverse intermediate events alongside recent motion under fixed memory. Because absolute temporal indices drift outside the training range, Bank-aware RoPE reassigns indices at attention time so each bank remains distinguishable. At 1.3B, Memory Forcing leads on longer clips, shows the smallest drop from 5s to 60s among methods reporting all four lengths, and preserves subjects and scenes through leave-and-return. The same design scales to Wan2.2 5B, producing more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos and, to our knowledge, the first public 5B model on this forcing line.
title: Memory Forcing: Attendable Mid-Horizon History for Streaming Video Generation

summary: LLM agents can spend millions of tokens during vulnerability discovery without producing a working proof of concept (PoC). What consumes that budget, and why does it fail to produce results? We diagnose these costs and failures through a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces, spanning four agents (i.e., Codex, OpenCode, Cybench, and EnIGMA) under an unaided baseline and four existing efficiency methods. The study reveals three key findings. First, different agents vary substantially in success and cost, and higher spending does not consistently yield better outcomes. Second, code localization and understanding, together with vulnerability reasoning and trigger design, account for 60.4% of tokens and represent the two leading bottlenecks in failed runs. Third, only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; unsuitable signals and auxiliary overhead limit the benefits of existing methods. Motivated by these findings, we present AVRI, an Agent-centric Vulnerability Reasoning Interface built around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET). BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
title: Where Do the Tokens Go? Understanding and Reducing Costs in LLM Agents for Vulnerability Discovery

summary: We establish the overarching mathematical physics framework underlying gravitational screening and electroweak mixing in Big Boot Gauge Theory (BBGT). To demonstrate that the transition from the bare gravitational constant G_bare = 6.514085763e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (derived from CODATA 2022 constants under unit space-time momentum p = mc = 1 kg m s^-1) to the observed value G_obs = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 is a rigorous topological necessity rather than an arbitrary post-hoc adjustment, we formulate the screening dynamics using Möbius inversion on finite posets over the subgroup lattice of Poincaré Dodecahedral Space (S^3/I^*). We prove that non-associative transit across the e_4 Pati-Salam midpoint node acts as a Möbius topological twist, fixing the geometric inverse-square screening factor S_ZIP^-2 = (1 - 1/120)^-2 = 1.016877348. Combining this with longitudinal Z-leakage (delta_Z = 0.026892000) and non-associative midpoint transit corrections (Delta_assoc = 0.000092701) yields the exact screened laboratory constant without arbitrary tuning.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak mixing angle (sin^2 theta_W = 1/5 + 1/32 = 0.23125) originates from the pentagonal P_5 symmetry order of the dodecahedron combined with a 2^5 chiral energy cascade, agreeing with experiment (0.23122) to within 0.01%. Finally, we present the complete 8x8 Logical Transitive Index Matrix (T_{n->m}), showing how the 10^19 Planck-to-electroweak mass hierarchy is compressed down to a discrete compilation factor of 128.35 across the aethereal boot levels.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-two entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR) with depth and finds the depth at which it falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: The present study was undertaken to establish pharmacognostic standards and phytochemical profiles of two ethnomedicinally important plants, Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii. Both species are traditionally employed in the treatment of rheumatism, inflammatory disorders, and other systemic ailments, yet scientific validation of their crude drug parameters remains limited. Standardization of herbal materials is essential to ensure identity, purity, and reproducibility, thereby reducing variability and enhancing therapeutic reliability. In this study, plant materials were procured from authentic local sources—Cajanus goensis from Udaipur, Rajasthan, and Sarcostigma kleinii from Latur, Maharashtra—and subjected to comprehensive pharmacognostic and phytochemical evaluation. Organoleptic analysis revealed distinct sensory characteristics, with Cajanus goensis exhibiting greenish-brown coloration, earthy odor, and coarse texture, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed yellowish-brown coloration, pungent odor, and oily texture. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed diagnostic features such as dorsiventral leaves, reticulate venation, thick cuticular layers, and prominent vascular bundles. Physico-chemical evaluation demonstrated that ash values, extractive values, moisture content, and pH were within pharmacopoeial limits, thereby confirming the purity and stability of the crude drugs. Notably, Cajanus goensis exhibited higher alcohol-soluble extractives, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed greater water-soluble extractives, reflecting differences in phytoconstituent solubility. Phytochemical screening revealed the presence of carbohydrates, amino acids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, tannins, and phenolic compounds in both species. Proteins were detected only in Sarcostigma kleinii, while saponins were present exclusively in Cajanus goensis. Sterols were absent in both plants, highlighting unique chemical signatures that aid in authentication. Quantitative estimation confirmed that both species are rich in flavonoids and phenolic compounds, with Sarcostigma kleinii showing slightly higher concentrations (21.06 ± 1.000 mg/g quercetin equivalents and 21.19 ± 0.854 mg/g tannic acid equivalents) compared to Cajanus goensis (19.09 ± 0.444 mg/g and 18.49 ± 0.033 mg/g, respectively). These bioactive constituents are well recognized for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, supporting the traditional use of these plants in rheumatism and related disorders. In conclusion, the study provides reproducible pharmacognostic and phytochemical data for Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii, thereby validating their ethnomedicinal claims and establishing a foundation for further pharmacological investigations. The results underscore the importance of standardization in herbal medicine and highlight the potential of these crude drugs as reliable sources of bioactive compounds for future therapeutic applications.
tags: Cajanus goensis; Sarcostigma kleinii; crude drug standardization; phytochemical screening; flavonoids; phenolic compounds; rheumatism; pharmacognosy; herbal medicine; quality control.
title: Standardization And Phytochemical Profiling of Cajanus Goensis and Sarcostigma Kleinii: Establishing Baseline Parameters for Crude Drug Evaluation

Authors: Yufan Chen, Zizhen Xu, Shauhrat S. Chopra
title: Data & Code for "Industrial symbiosis networks require different structural strategies to remain resilient across sizes"

summary: World models for control must capture which aspects of the environment respond to the agent's actions and which are relevant to reward. Generative world models such as Dreamer 4 consist of a video tokenizer, which encodes each frame into a latent, and a dynamics model, which is pretrained to predict future latents from past latents and actions. Yet the tokenizer is trained with a reconstruction objective, without action or reward supervision, so its latent provides no explicit mechanism to separate controllable, uncontrollable, reward-relevant, and reward-irrelevant information. We propose \textit{CausalDreamer}, which keeps the tokenizer frozen and re-encodes its latent into a factored representation of four groups along two axes: controllability, where only the two controllable groups receive the action, and reward relevance, learned by predicting the reward from the two reward-relevant groups. The pretrained dynamics model is then fine-tuned to predict the factored representation. We evaluate \textit{CausalDreamer} and the pretrained world model it starts from with model-predictive planning on 20 MMBench2 tasks: 10 clean tasks seen during training and 10 unseen tasks, of which 6 are manipulated variants of clean tasks with a changed background, object, or maze layout, and 4 are new environments. We normalize returns so that a policy taking uniformly random actions scores 0 and an expert scores 1. \textit{CausalDreamer} achieves a 14\% higher normalized score than the pretrained world model on the clean tasks (0.199 vs.\ 0.175) and a 25\% higher score on the manipulated variants (0.307 vs.\ 0.246), while neither model scores meaningfully above the random policy in the new environments. Additionally, our analysis shows that the factored representation separates reward-irrelevant changes, such as a changed background, from its reward-relevant groups.
title: CausalDreamer: Learning Predictive World Models with Latent Disentanglement

summary: Modern neural networks are heavily over-parameterized. This redundancy incurs substantial compute and memory overhead during training and inference. Existing pruning methods rely on post-hoc magnitude thresholds or static initialization heuristics. Consequently, they often require manual per-layer sparsity targets or expensive retraining cycles. We propose Dynamic Activity-Dependent Pruning (DADP), a biologically inspired structural plasticity mechanism. During training, DADP measures connection importance via the accumulated product of pre-synaptic activations and post-synaptic error gradients. Using a single global threshold instead of fixed layer budgets, DADP dynamically allocates sparsity across network depth while naturally inducing neuron- and channel-level pruning. Across MLP, VGG-16, ResNet-18, BiLSTM-CRF, and MiniBERT architectures, DADP matches or outperforms Magnitude, SNIP and RigL, retaining 73.67% accuracy (dense baseline: 76.06%) at 99% sparsity on ResNet-18. Finally, matrix-based Shannon entropy and effective rank measurements confirm that DADP preserves latent feature diversity at extreme sparsities without representation collapse.
title: DADP: Dynamic Activity-Dependent Pruning, A Reverse Hebbian-Inspired Structural Pruning Method

summary: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits: 1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM's latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model. 3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.
title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC

summary: Understanding a dynamical world calls for more than a latent state that summarizes its observations: the state should also be organized into the factors that stay shared across related observations and the factors that vary between them. For example, a robot pushing a cube to a goal should take the same action when the camera shifts or the lights dim, since nothing in the scene has moved. Existing approaches to this decomposition commonly obtain it through reconstruction, so the latent variables must first explain the entire observational world before their organization can be trusted. Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) model the latent state directly and never reconstruct, yet no existing result recovers the invariant and variant parts of the state they learn. How to learn the invariant-variant structure of the latent world without paying for its reconstruction therefore remains open. To close this gap, we introduce SplitJEPA, a JEPA that jointly recovers the latent state and its invariant and variant organization directly in representation space, without any reconstruction. We prove that, under stationary Gaussian predictive dynamics and a full-rank variation condition, SplitJEPA identifies the invariant and variant subspaces up to independent block-wise isometries, without introducing an observation decoder. Since the guarantee needs no decoder, the result extends reconstruction-free latent recovery to invariant-variant block identification. Experiments on synthetic nonlinear systems and robotic manipulation tasks support the theoretical results and show their practical value for both robustness and efficiency.
title: SplitJEPA: Learning Invariant and Variant Latent Worlds without Reconstruction

summary: We identify explicit closed-form and variational formulae for interpolating the exact values and derivatives through order $s$ of a $C^{s,1}$ function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ at $N$ distinct points in $[0,1]^d$. The reconstruction satisfies bounds on its global $C^{s,1}$ seminorm and its Lipschitz constant on $[0,1]^d$ that are independent of the sample size $N$, the latter being the sharp Whitney condition. For $s\ge2$, the reconstruction is real analytic away from the data points and definable in the o-minimal structure $\mathbb{R}_{\exp}$. Our nonlinear extension formula coincides with the formula of McShane (1934) for $s=0$ and with the formulae of Le Gruyer and Phan (2015) and Azagra, Le Gruyer, and Mudarra (2018) for $s=1$, and is new for $s\ge2$. For fixed $d$ and $s\ge2$, our closed-form formula is computable away from the data points by a circuit using only elementary unary and binary real operations, with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ gates and $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ depth. This yields $\mathcal{O}(N)$ storage and $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ parallel evaluation time. From the supplied coefficients and weights, the circuit can be compiled with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ one-time work in the exact-real word-RAM model. Thus, in this supplied-data setting, our nonlinear construction improves by a logarithmic factor on the $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$ initialization bound of Fefferman and Klartag (2009), while retaining linear storage and attaining logarithmic query time through parallel evaluation.
title: A Computationally-Efficient Closed-Form $C^{s,1}$-Extension Formula

summary: It is assumed that a natural way to improve the pedagogical quality of large language model tutors is to define a metric of instructional performance and fine-tune the model against it. To test this strategy, we designed a metric of pedagogical adaptivity that scores each instructional decision in a learning sequence against the conditions of the learning situation, which is the standard used for automated pedagogical scoring. We audited a frontier tutor across 2,000 learner scenarios, corrected its weakest cases by fine-tuning an open-weights proxy, and asked 31 trained educators to rate the pedagogical alignment of the outputs blind, before and after correction. The metric increased from +0.05 to +0.42 for the corrected cases, while the expert ratings decreased from 4.46 to 3.03, with the unmodified controls remaining unchanged and a base-proxy control ruling out the change of model. The tutor performed worse because any metric that scores decisions independently and averages them is maximized by repeating the single best decision, and the fine-tuned model collapsed to that exact optimum in every case, in and out of sample. Educators identified the repetition, which such metrics cannot represent, and preserving the learner's trajectory in the score reduced, but did not reverse, the metric's verdict. Weight analysis traced the correction to the model's output projection, where it had memorized its training strings rather than learned to adapt. We conclude that measurement validity does not imply optimization validity, and we derive design principles for benchmarks that assess or train AI-tutor instruction.
title: The learner who does not learn: when optimizing a pedagogical metric degrades LLM tutoring

summary: This paper develops a new predefined-time integral reinforcement learning framework for optimal control of unknown nonlinear systems. The unknown drift is first approximated by a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, together with a data-driven online identification law for updating the corresponding neural weights. After the identifier converges to a sufficiently small neighborhood of the true dynamics, the learned model is incorporated into the integral reinforcement learning (IRL) problem. Unlike conventional reinforcement-learning-based optimal control, the desired convergence time is introduced directly into the control objective: a Lyapunov function and its prescribed decay behavior are specified by the designer, and inverse-optimal control is then used to construct a compatible running cost whose optimal policy inherits the predefined-time stabilization property. The value function is approximated by a second RBF neural network, and a new critic update law is developed to impose predefined-time convergence on the critic weights. Finite informative learning data are stored in a replay buffer and reused during the critic update, thereby avoiding the need for persistent excitation throughout the closed-loop operation. Theoretical analysis proves that the critic-weight error enters a prescribed residual set within the allocated learning horizon, while the closed-loop state reaches a small neighborhood of the origin within the overall designer-specified deadline. Numerical simulations on an unknown nonlinear system verify accurate drift reconstruction, predefined-time critic learning, and closed-loop convergence.
title: Predefined-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Systems via Inverse-Optimal Design

summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations

summary: Flux emergence is often accompanied by flux cancellation, which may drive dynamic phenomena in the solar atmosphere. We studied magnetic flux cancellation in a three-dimensional resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of an emerging flux tube with a non-uniform twist profile. We solved time-dependent resistive MHD equations to model flux emergence into a magnetised background atmosphere. We identified several cancellation sites, estimated their cancellation rates, and examined the magnetic topology and associated jet activity. The non-uniform twist produced multiple opposite photospheric polarities, leading to a complex multipolar magnetic configuration rather than a simple dipolar structure. Interactions between inner secondary magnetic patches resulted in flux cancellation of the photospheric $B_z$ along their polarity inversion line (PIL). These interactions led to the formation of concave-up loops and a cancellation rate of $1.1 \times 10^{19}$ Mx hr$^{-1}$. During cancellation, magnetic reconnection between converging opposite polarities progressively created a coherent magnetic flux rope above the cancellation region. The evolution of the rope was associated with a blowout jet, as the rope expanded and released part of its stored twist into the overlying corona. We also examined two smaller secondary cancellation events at photospheric heights. Our results highlight the role of internal flux cancellation in restructuring the magnetic field and driving blowout-jet activity in emerging regions.
title: Magnetic flux cancellation in a 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an emerging flux tube with a non-uniform twist

summary: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
title: Escaping Geological Generative Prior Distributions in Bayesian Travel Time Tomography

summary: Structure-preserving numerical methods for gradient flows have been extensively developed when the governing equations and free energies are known. However, accurately predicting dynamics from observational data while preserving intrinsic physical properties remains challenging. Although neural operators, such as Fourier neural operators (FNOs), provide powerful data-driven approximations, their predictions do not inherently guarantee physical structure preservation. To address this challenge, we integrate deep learning with structure-preserving exponential time differencing (ETD) methods. Instead of directly learning the evolution operator, we introduce a *trajectory-inferred free energy* (TIFE), which reconstructs the unknown energy density from observed trajectories through a Duhamel-based learning framework. The learned energy determines the variational force and stabilization parameter, enabling structure-preserving numerical evolution. We further extend the framework to jointly identify the free energy and diffusion coefficient. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the maximum-bound principle, unconditional dissipation of the original learned energy, and error estimates incorporating discretization and inference errors. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate energy recovery and reliable long-time predictions.
title: Data-Driven Free-Energy Learning from Trajectories via Structure-Preserving Exponential Time Differencing

summary: We study the relation between equal-weight circle quadrature, Gauss--Chebyshev quadrature, and planar Minkowski reconstruction. The regular $N$-point grid is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$; a half-step rotation of the $2M$-point grid projects to the classical $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule. A common family of quadrature-error functionals gives exact identities for integration error, mixed-area error, and support-function error. For $N\ge3$, the centered Minkowski polygon $P_N$ with perimeter $2π$ has the exact Hausdorff distance from the unit disk $B^2$ \[ d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-\fracπ{N}\cot\fracπ{N} =\frac{π^2}{3N^2}+O(N^{-4}). \] With Steiner centering, we obtain $d_H(K_μ,K_ν)\leπW_1(μ,ν)$ for balanced, nondegenerate probability measures, where $W_1$ uses geodesic distance. Its exponent is sharp even for smooth positive densities near the uniform measure. The identity $W_1(ν_N,σ)=π/(2N)$ yields a general $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the regular grid. The sharper $O(N^{-2})$ rate follows from the sparse discrepancy spectrum and the inverse multiplier $(1-k^2)^{-1}$. Finally, a perturbation estimate gives sufficient conditions for preserving the quadratic rate and its leading constant.
title: Gauss--Chebyshev Quadrature, $\mathbb S^1$-Designs, and the Planar Minkowski Inverse Problem: A One-Dimensional Model for Design-Induced Convex Geometry

summary: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act , the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation , supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV) . For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation ind
title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

summary: Dense associative memory (DAM) provides an energy-based framework for memory retrieval with close connections to attention mechanisms in modern artificial intelligence. Despite growing interest in differential privacy for AI, the privacy of DAM retrieval dynamics remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we develop a differential privacy framework for log-sum-ReLU (LSR) dense associative memory, whose finite-support retrieval dynamics pose distinctive challenges for privacy-preserving computation. We propose the Boundary-Responsive Adaptive Correction Evolution (BRACE) algorithm, a differentially private retrieval mechanism for LSR-DAM that adaptively corrects boundary-sensitive perturbations to control their cumulative effect over the retrieval trajectory. In theory, we prove that our method is minimax optimal by deriving dimension-independent terminal and full-trajectory retrieval error rates, with optimal dependence on the inverse temperature and, in the growing-horizon regime, the retrieval horizon. We further establish central limit theorems that enable uncertainty quantification for private retrieval by characterizing its asymptotic distribution and the additional variability introduced by privacy. Numerical experiments compare our proposed method with baseline differential privacy approaches and evaluate its retrieval accuracy. Together, our results provide a theoretical foundation for optimal privacy-preserving retrieval and uncertainty quantification in energy-based associative memory systems.
title: BRACE: Differential Privacy for Dense Associative Memory with LSR Energy

summary: Robotic manipulation often contains repeated motions whose local observations look similar at different phases. When these phases require different actions, a policy that relies mainly on the current observation may repeat completed motions or switch phases at the wrong time. To address this phase ambiguity, we present the Pseudo-Memory Temporal Re-encoding Module (PMTRM), a lightweight plug-in module with only 7.61M parameters that encodes a bounded history of executed states and actions into a latent sequence for existing policies. To help distinguish phases, a temporal heterogeneity objective penalizes positive similarity between distant positions in this sequence, while anchor and reconstruction losses preserve information needed for action prediction. The reconstruction decoder is used only during training, leaving the temporal re-encoder to supply history to the policy at inference. We train the module progressively on synthetic sequences and robot data, then jointly with the policy, using temporal masking to accommodate partial histories. This integration retains the original action head and action space and adds auxiliary losses to the original policy loss. Experiments with multiple policy backbones in simulation and on a real robot show improved task success on tasks with phase ambiguity, with little additional computation.
title: PMTRM: Pseudo-Memory Temporal Re-encoding Module for Embodied Policy Learning

summary: The Tensor-Memory Equilibrium (TME) model of "FP8 is All You Need (Part 1)" calculates the execution time of Ozaki Scheme II emulation of fp64 as the maximum of a tensor-core term and a High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic term, plus a per-output reconstruction term. However, it omits the per-input deconstruction cost: every streamed fp64 operand must be scaled, rounded, and reduced modulo each of the $r$ moduli on SIMT pipes before any matrix multiply can issue. In this note we add this fourth term, calibrate its constant from the cuBLAS emulation path, and derive a closed-form operational-intensity threshold $\mathrm{OI}^{*} = c_q r P_{\mathrm{fp64}}/(8P_{\mathrm{int}})$ below which emulation cannot match native fp64 regardless of tensor-core throughput. On the NVIDIA B300 GPU the threshold is $\mathrm{OI}^{*}\approx 0.56$ FLOP/B. As a result, GEMV, SpMV, and low-batch GEMV, which are the memory-bound kernels the original paper claims to accelerate, are limited to 0.3-0.9x of native performance, and the 7-point stencil to 1.8x rather than the claimed 3.1x. Dense GEMM is unaffected as expected. We also show that precomputing and storing the residues moves the same cost into the bandwidth term, and we state the instruction count that an implementation would have to achieve to invalidate the bound.
title: The Missing Fourth Term for the Emulation Tensor Memory Equilibrium (TME) Model: The Residue Deconstruction Cost

summary: Long-term agents face growing storage demands as they accumulate experience. World models capture reusable regularities that can reduce the information stored for each experience. We formulate the problem of memory allocation conditioned on a world model and introduce MemoWM, a framework that uses shared predictions to compress retained information and reconstruct omitted content. Its task-aware allocation rule balances the expected impact of reconstruction errors against storage cost, retaining information with downstream value beyond the predictive prior. Across five long-term agent-memory benchmarks, MemoWM achieves 42.42\% average answer accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.62 percentage points, while reducing average experience-specific storage by 53.9\% relative to MIRIX, the most storage-efficient baseline. Further analysis shows that stronger world models reduce per-experience storage at comparable task quality. Accounting for model parameters reveals a trade-off between shared model capacity and recurring storage costs, with the capacity that minimizes total storage increasing as more interactions are retained. Our code is available at https://github.com/Feld-maxiu/MemoWM.
title: MemoWM: How World Models Change What Agents Need to Remember

summary: Supporting research data for physical-state supervision of design-only Gaussian process surrogates, with optional mixture-of-experts comparisons. Includes 1,987 CH designs, 3,000 thermal-explosion designs, 3,000 recalculated Be/Cocktail designs, state diagnostics, saved predictions, paired evaluation metrics, learning curves, grid diagnostics, timing records and file-level provenance. The data record does not include software, solver binaries, material libraries or raw trajectories. Grid sensitivities and historical reproduction limitations are documented in README.md. Data and accompanying documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0.
title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations: supporting data

summary: Self-contained computational materials accompanying "Verifiable approval-release decisions for construction project management: A provenance-aware contract and automated evidence" by Ahmad Baghdadi. Version 4.0.0 includes source code, complete generated inputs and results, schemas, exact witnesses, a de-identified calendar encoding, benchmark records and SHA-256 checksums. This version adds 83 conventional priority-list levelling comparisons under identical constraints: 72 tied peaks and 11 one-gate improvements, with sufficient exact certificates for all 83. A complete two-plan PROV-O example passes the domain and provenance SHACL profiles and preserves every decision field after RDF exchange. The suite comprises 145 automated tests. Earlier computational evidence includes generated extraction, 360 controlled record comparisons, exact wave bounds, nine calendar scenarios and 80 saved benchmark plans with renewed arithmetic audit. S14 preparation includes blank independent-annotation and approval registers plus a precision/recall evaluator with explicit denominators. No native baseline or independent annotations are available; field validation has not been executed. Case A remains historical aggregates only. Calendar B is a prior encoding with assumed review windows. Supplementary Table S1 identifies the deposited components and the supplement consolidates the evidence limits.
title: Reproducibility materials for verifiable approval-release decisions in construction project management

summary: A book in progress on agentic coding and agentic research, compiled from the repository that is its evidence, written around one problem: moving the expensive kernels of the WAVEWATCH III (WW3) third-generation spectral wind-wave model to GPUs without changing the answer. Seventeen lessons, built into a PDF on every merge, from the wave spectrum to running the Fortran model on real cases with a pinned Nix toolchain and annotated switch files. Benchmarks on CPU (OpenMP, MPI) and GPU (OpenACC, CUDA Fortran), each number with the command that reproduces it. A C++/Kokkos port of W3SNL1, the Discrete Interaction Approximation (DIA) of nonlinear four-wave interactions, written with coding agents and shown bit-identical to the Fortran on the Serial, OpenMP and CUDA backends by a field-by-field parity harness. The method itself: the rules coding agents follow here, design docs with a definition of done (WFIPs), decision records (ADRs), a research log, and plans whose every claim carries its evidence. Includes runnable examples, exercises with solutions, and an undergraduate project proposal (Escola Politécnica, UFRJ, co-advised at LabECO, UFSC).
title: WW3 GPU Lab: agentic coding and agentic research on a bit-for-bit GPU port of WAVEWATCH III

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a comment on a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview and comments at https://prereview.org/reviews/22745390 . Thank you, Evgenii, for the detailed and constructive PREreview. Your comments led us to substantially strengthen both the experimental design and the interpretation of the results. We have now released a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the main points raised in the review. The revision includes: A 30-seed robustness analysis rather than relying on a single simulation seed A correlation sweep for estimator errors from ρ = 0 to 0.8 Regression-fitted and test-set oracle aggregation baselines Shared-noise experiments for the model–collective calibration signal, reported with ROC-AUC and lift Explicit specification of the four-Wave rolling calibration window, software versions, and PCG64 RNG Portfolio scaling to 100 Feature Blocks using an exact binary MILP reference An explicit separation between budget-constrained portfolio selection and ODP's native dependency-aware sequencing role An exact and scaling benchmark for ODP sequencing under prerequisite constraints An explicit competing-interest disclosure A public reproducibility package containing the simulation code, deterministic seeds, generated data, analysis scripts, and validation material. One particularly useful outcome of the revision was that the stronger experiments narrowed some of our original claims. For example, inverse-MSE aggregation performs very strongly when estimator errors are independent, but its advantage collapses under strong shared error. We also found that ODP distance is not the strongest heuristic for budget-constrained portfolio selection, while it performs very differently in its native sequencing role, where ERS/BVS is exactly optimal for the declared objective without dependencies and remains close to the exact optimum under the tested prerequisite constraints. Revised manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10648 Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23261325 Thank you again for the review. It improved the paper. Competing interests I am a co-author of the manuscript discussed in this PREreview and a contributor to the D-POAF framework evaluated in the study. I am also affiliated with Inovionix, which develops software implementing D-POAF concepts.
title: Comment on a PREreview of "Governed Human-AI Prioritization Under Uncertainty: Adaptive Estimation and Dependency-Constrained Portfolio Selection"

summary: Anatomical continuity provides complementary information for medical image restoration, but its use requires accounting for local anatomy and variations in slice sampling. We introduce ContiLNN, which augments two-dimensional restoration backbones with bidirectional closed-form continuous-time (Bi-CfC) modules for cross-slice modeling while retaining in-plane feature extraction. Slice-index intervals modulate gates determined by local features and hidden states, enabling propagation to respond to sampling variations without numerical ODE integration. Reference-guided consistency aligns first- and second-order cross-slice intensity differences to preserve anatomical variation, while distillation from a frozen backbone helps retain in-plane fidelity. Across five training seeds, ContiLNN improves mean PSNR over Restore-RWKV by 0.1907, 1.0176, and 1.2482 dB for CT denoising, MRI super-resolution, and reduced-count PET restoration, respectively, with lower RMSE in all three tasks. CT results are descriptive for one held-out patient. PET ablations support ordered propagation beyond additional pointwise capacity. Under contiguous training, Bi-CfC achieves higher fidelity than a Bi-GRU with similar parameter counts and arithmetic costs across all tested sampling conditions. Matched seven-slice profiling shows 52.8% lower latency and 57.0% lower peak GPU memory use than Bi-GRU. Mixed-gap training improves sparse and irregular-context performance for both operators, without a uniform ranking across metrics and contexts. Experiments with fewer training patients and a second backbone further support data efficiency and backbone compatibility.
title: ContiLNN: Mitigating Slice Sampling Discontinuity with Liquid Neural Networks for Medical Image Restoration

summary: While the volume of preserved research data and analysis software has grown significantly over the last decade, much of this valuable asset remains siloed in national or thematic repositories, in heterogeneous data and metadata formats that make dataset integration difficult. As a consequence, valuable scientific insights remain unexplored as researchers should spend increasing amounts of time with data discovery, interpretation, formatting and transformation. EOSC Data Commons (EDC) is building the next-generation federated research data infrastructure to eliminate cross-repository and cross-format data fragmentation. At the centre of the EDC technical architecture there are two complementary services, designed to bridge disconnected systems: EOSC Matchmaker: a discovery layer enabling researchers to discover datasets, software tools, and execution services across multiple scientific domains and EOSC Nodes. It operates alongside a catalogue of analytics tools that can be deployed close to the data, significantly reducing data movement and improving processing efficiency. EOSC Data Player: An execution platform integration service that provides harmonised APIs, shared metadata specifications, and common mechanisms for authentication, authorisation, and provenance tracking. This ensures that researchers can combine data and software tools from different providers without manually reconciling metadata formats or security protocols. To achieve scalable interoperability, the project uses a range of advanced semantic technologies, including knowledge graphs for rich metadata representation and standardised interfaces to support cross-infrastructure integration. EOSC Data Commons adopts community standards such as RO-Crate for packaging research artefacts and their metadata in a machine-actionable, highly interoperable manner. This technical stack is continuously validated through real-world use cases spanning diverse scientific domains. For data repositories, the technical frameworks established by EOSC Data Commons offer a highly practical blueprint. Testing EDC’s technological ecosystem through its open call, national repositories, such as ARP, can integrate with the broader European Open Science Cloud and expand their reach into new scientific communities, while maintaining their operational autonomy and data security. This presentation outlines the core technological solutions, semantic standards, and interoperability frameworks developed by EDC to enable seamless, cross-disciplinary data reuse. The talk aims to generate interest in the Hungarian ARP community to join the growing network of EDC repositories.
title: The Missing Link of EOSC: Interoperability of Data Repositories and Applications with EOSC Data Commons

summary: Vehicle motion forecasters use surrounding agents as interaction context, but a bounded context requires choosing which K agents to retain. Geometric rules capture traffic structure without accounting for how a predictor uses it. We define relevance through a frozen forecaster's leave-one-agent-out (LOO) prediction sensitivity: the change in its output when one agent is removed. An offline LOO teacher is distilled into a parameter scorer that ranks candidates from frozen embeddings and pairwise kinematics in one scorer pass. Selection occurs after candidate encoding and before aggregation, imposing a context budget while retaining the shared encoder and decoder. On NGSIM (Next Generation Simulation) US-101 with causal preprocessing and recording-level splits, lane structure explains most of the margin over proximity. Against lane-aware selection at the last observed frame, the student reduces average displacement error (ADE) by m with max-pooling and m with attention pooling across the original three seeds. Uniform scorer retraining across five seeds favors the student in four of five runs for each aggregation. Relative to initial-frame proximity, the max-pool student gains m at validation-locked K= (student-minus-proximity 95% CI m). Objectives and reporting capacities are fixed on validation data using common candidate pools. Saliency gives similar primary max-pool ADE; capacity-matched ADE-trained attention remains competitive. The analysis relates discrepancy to ADE, establishes exact LOO top-K surrogate minimization and ranking stability, and separates student ranking loss from non-additive approximation error. Exhaustive subset analysis on scenes per seed shows useful selections despite a loose surrogate and tight margins. On inD and rounD, teacher margins over proximity and student gains are negligible. Sensitivity distillation provides a predictor-specific selection signal beyond geometry; its accuracy advantage depends on the aggregation mechanism and dataset. Code, checkpoints and numerical provenance support reproduction.
title: Model-aware neighbor selection for vehicle motion forecasting via leave-one-agent-out sensitivity distillation

summary: Complete Lean formalization of the actual-state qutrit–qudit APPT maximal-purity theorem, for every integer n >= 3. Exact theorem The maximum of Tr(rho^2) over trace-one positive semidefinite complex matrices on C^3 tensor C^n that remain PPT after every global unitary conjugation is: (3n+8)/(3n+2)^2 for 3 <= n <= 8; 3/(8n) for n >= 9. APPT.Quantum.appt_purity_maximum_formula states this as IsGreatest , including both the universal upper bound and a physical APPT attaining state. There are no unproved spectral, corner-PSD, or Hildebrand-equivalence assumptions in the final statement. Verification All 879 local modules and the default Lake build passed. All 18 regeneration, build, paired positive/negative, and kernel-audit stages passed. 155,787 declarations / 58 roots were replayed in an initially empty kernel at trust level zero . The only axioms are propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound . The same final theorem was tested with its proof replaced by True.intro ; the fresh kernel rejected it for a declaration type mismatch. The changed declaration's 8,581 type/proof dependencies were positively checked separately. No sorry , admit , custom axiom, or untrusted native_decide occurs in the verified mathematical proof closure. All module builds were bounded by 300 seconds; the largest recorded module took 239.703 seconds. Verification run: https://github.com/mxym/math/actions/runs/37968137659 Verified source commit: f372047c63ba501b13301b4b3ba089c261e3722e . Publication commit: 2fc3f25179cf1128c4bccbde65fd3a07c093ad6d . The final CI reuses independently compiled source/object-hash-bound component builds; it does not claim a fresh 879-module build on one runner. The complete original mathematical proof closure is nonetheless rechecked independently from an empty kernel. The source package supports a fresh build with python3 reproduce.py --fresh --jobs 2 . Reproduce Use Lean 4.34.1 , with Mathlib pinned to d13f23b723b8a846827a245b89c10fc7d3f11612 . Extract the source archive and run from its package root: lake exe cache get python3 scripts/source_manifest.py --check python3 reproduce.py --fresh --jobs 2 The source archive contains all 942 pinned proof/tool/data files, the exact certificates, deterministic generators, a paper-to-Lean proof map, and verification scripts. The verification archive retains literal logs, source hashes, root/axiom inventories, component provenance, and the original full CI artifact. RELEASE_MANIFEST.json binds both archives to the verified and published sources; SHA256SUMS gives transport hashes. Scope and preserved history This release completes the specified purity theorem for all n >= 3. It does not claim a classification of all maximizers, arbitrary first-factor dimension, a separability optimum, novelty/priority, or external peer review. The physical necessity and direct attainment proofs avoid assuming a full Hildebrand if-and-only-if theorem. The immutable appt-qutrit-purity-interim-v1 Release and its source tree/assets are unchanged. Earlier failed audit attempts are retained as failed records, not relabeled as successes.
title: mxym/math: Qutrit–qudit APPT purity: complete all-n Lean proof v1

summary: Replication package for a validation study of three off-the-shelf sentiment instruments (SenticNet 9, VADER, Twitter-RoBERTa) against blind three-coder human annotation on a stratified audit sample of 504 tweets, drawn from a collection of English-language tweets directed at six European airlines in the summers of 2018-2022 (252,650 user tweets after removal of re-captured records). The package contains, with no tweet text: tweet-level labels of all three instruments for every collected record (re-captured records and truncated author identifiers flagged); the 504 audited items with all three coders' original ratings, the original majority consensus, the post-audit adjudications and completed ratings, and a text-free linkage summary of each audited item's capture multiplicity; the codebook; the VADER and Twitter-RoBERTa scorers with the model revision; a conda environment manifest; and a single script (code/reproduce_all.py) that regenerates every statistic in the manuscript's tables, including the multiplicity-adjusted stratified difference estimates.
